title: Converge worktree detection on one primitive
description:
Worktree detection and primary-checkout discovery answer from one primitive instead of five
independent implementations.

## Background

Five separate implementations currently decide whether the current checkout is a linked
non-primary worktree and where the primary checkout lives: a version-control layout probe
computed before every dispatch, a test for whether the repository pointer is a file in the
JSON storage backend, a library-level path comparison in index loading, an inline
version-control invocation in issue loading, and a linked-checkout fallback in the
repository-state store. They can disagree, and nothing names one of them as authoritative.
The layout probe is the most complete and is already computed before dispatch, so it becomes
the single answer.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: One primitive answers whether the selected data root sits inside a linked non-primary checkout and where the primary checkout's store is; no second implementation of either question survives in storage or command code.
- [hard] REQ-02: Outside version control the primitive reports a non-linked checkout rather than failing, so repositories without version control keep working.
- [hard] REQ-03: When an environment override selects the data root, classification follows that selected root's location rather than the process working directory, and that behaviour is covered.
- [hard] REQ-04: The layered issue read fallback, the deletion policy, and worktree introspection keep their current observable behaviour while reading the converged primitive.

## Notes

The read-side layered issue resolution (local store, then version-control history, then the
primary checkout) is documented adopter-facing behaviour and is unchanged here; only the
detection question underneath it converges.

planning.outcome: One primitive answers whether this checkout is linked and where the primary store lives.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: Five known implementations converge onto one primitive that already runs before every dispatch, adding no new behaviour outside the storage and dispatch layers.

title: Worktree write policy configuration key
description:
Repository configuration declares whether state-mutating commands may run inside a linked
non-primary checkout, and resolves to refusal when nothing is declared.

## Background

The configuration already carries a worktree section whose lease-enforcement key is typed,
parsed at load, and defaulted in one place. A write-policy stance follows that same shape: a
typed value with a stated default, so a repository chooses its stance in version-controlled
configuration rather than through an undeclared environment convention. The shipped default
refuses, because the adopter who never considered the question is the one the divergent-store
hazard hurts.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A typed write-policy value parses from the worktree configuration section and rejects unknown tokens at load time with a message naming the accepted ones.
- [hard] REQ-02: With no declared value, and with no worktree section at all, the resolved stance refuses state-mutating commands inside a linked non-primary checkout.
- [hard] REQ-03: A declared permissive stance resolves to permitting those commands, and the precedence between the declared stance and a per-invocation override is stated once and covered by tests.
- [hard] REQ-04: This repository declares the permissive stance in its own tracker configuration, so its linked agent checkouts keep mutating their local stores.
- [hard] REQ-05: The configuration reference states the key, its accepted values, its default, and how an absent section resolves, worded as the repository's declared stance rather than as a promise of enforcement.

## Notes

The neighbouring lease-enforcement key resolves differently depending on whether the section
is present at all. The write-policy key states its own resolution explicitly rather than
inheriting that asymmetry.

planning.outcome: A typed worktree policy key resolves the mutation stance for linked checkouts, defaulting to refusal.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One typed key parsed beside an existing key in the same configuration section, with its default resolution and its reference entry.

title: Converge mutation-context construction onto one factory
description:
Production mutation contexts are constructed through one factory instead of twenty-two
independent constructor calls spread across fourteen command modules, with behaviour
unchanged.

## Background

The production mutation context — the injected authority and clock a finalized plan derives
its identifiers and timestamp from — is constructed independently wherever a command needs
one. A fact decided once at dispatch has no way to reach those contexts without either
threading through the modules one by one or converging their construction first. Convergence
is the shared-convention remedy: one factory owns production-context construction and carries
an optional dispatch-scoped annotation slot, empty by default, so a later change can set a
fact in one place and have it reach the finalizer through the context it already receives.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: One factory constructs the production mutation context, the per-module constructor calls route through it, and the direct constructor is no longer callable from command modules.
- [hard] REQ-02: The factory carries an optional dispatch-scoped annotation slot that is empty by default, and an empty slot changes no behaviour: no new events, identical outputs, identical persisted bytes for the same inputs.
- [hard] REQ-03: The full test suite passes unchanged apart from construction-site mechanics, demonstrating the convergence is behaviour-preserving.

planning.outcome: One factory owns production mutation-context construction, replacing twenty-two scattered constructor calls.

terminal.test_boundary: existing suite unchanged plus factory unit coverage
terminal.worker_sized_reason: Twenty-two mechanical constructor swaps onto one factory whose empty slot is behaviour-preserving; a single deliverable class with the existing suite pinning the no-change property.

title: Override audit event for linked-checkout mutations
description:
A permitted override of the linked-checkout write stance has its own event variant in the
closed event vocabulary, with the catalog and rendered-reference rows the freshness guard
requires.

## Background

The event vocabulary is a closed, serde-tagged model mirrored by a fieldless tag set, and a
freshness guard fails when a variant is missing from the catalog or the rendered event
reference. An ordinary mutation event cannot show that an invocation was permitted
specifically by an override rather than by a permissive stance, so the record needs a
distinct variant. This leaf defines the vocabulary only; how a record of this kind becomes
durable alongside the mutation it permits is a separate publication concern.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A distinct event variant records a permitted override of the linked-checkout write stance, naming the linked checkout, the stance that would have refused, and the override that permitted the invocation.
- [hard] REQ-02: The variant appears in the event catalog, the rendered event reference is regenerated from that catalog rather than edited by hand, and the existing freshness guard fails if either is missing.
- [hard] REQ-03: The variant round-trips through serialization with a stable type tag, and existing event-log readers tolerate and report it.

planning.outcome: The closed event vocabulary carries a distinct override-audit variant with catalog and reference conformance.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One event variant with its catalog row and reference row, following the conformance guard the event model already enforces; publication semantics are owned elsewhere.

title: Publish the override audit record with the mutation it permits
description:
A mutation permitted by an explicit override of the linked-checkout write stance becomes
durable together with its audit record through the same materialization plan; if the
application fails, neither lands.

## Background

Events become durable only when mutation intents are finalized into one materialization plan
and applied through the recovering transaction kernel; an event variant on its own publishes
nothing. The carrier therefore spans the whole path: the dispatch site that decides an
override permitted the invocation sets the fact once; the mutation context carries it to the
finalizer, whose event pass composes the audit append; and because the second finalizer path used for
initialization-style audit appends shares that same event-pass helper, one edit covers both
paths, so no materialization path can emit its events while omitting the record. This avoids threading the fact through the fourteen
command modules that construct production contexts.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A mutation permitted by an explicit override materializes its audit record in the same finalized plan as the mutation, and both become durable in one application.
- [hard] REQ-02: An injected persistence failure during that application leaves neither the mutation nor the audit record behind after recovery.
- [hard] REQ-03: On success, the audit record is readable from the event log alongside the mutation's own events, in canonical order.
- [hard] REQ-04: An invocation with no override in effect emits no audit record, so a repository that declares neither a stance nor an override sees no new events.
- [hard] REQ-05: The dispatch-set override fact reaches both finalizer paths that compose audit appends, with coverage that fails if a materialization path omits the record.

## Notes

The finalizer documents that a no-transition plan carries an empty delta and emits no bytes.
The audit record accompanies real events only: an override in effect during a no-op mutation
produces no record, preserving that documented property.

planning.outcome: An override-permitted mutation and its audit record become durable through one finalized plan, or neither lands.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One override fact carried along one seam — set at dispatch, read by the two finalizer paths that compose audit appends — with failure-injection coverage reusing the proven injector; no per-command threading.

title: Refuse state-mutating commands in linked worktrees
description:
A state-mutating invocation inside a linked non-primary checkout refuses before any repository
write unless the declared stance or an explicit override permits it.

## Background

The command enumeration already classifies every invocation by whether it must open a
repository mutation session. That classification is exhaustive over the command families that
delegate to a sub-enum classifier; five read-only families match their inner enum with a
wildcard, so a new mutating leaf under one of them must be classified deliberately rather than
inherited silently. That predicate, combined with the worktree primitive computed before
dispatch, is exactly the condition a write policy needs, and evaluating it before the
repository mutation session is opened leaves a refusal with no partial state and no event
behind. One command — issue deletion — already refuses in secondary checkouts today, evidence
that the dispatch site is where such a condition belongs.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Under the refusing stance, an invocation that would open a repository mutation session inside a linked non-primary checkout fails before any repository write, leaving that checkout's store and event log untouched.
- [hard] REQ-02: The refusal names the linked checkout, the stance that refused it, and how to permit the operation; its machine-readable form carries the same three facts.
- [hard] REQ-03: A permissive declared stance and an explicit per-invocation override each permit the invocation, and a permitted override leaves its durable audit record behind.
- [hard] REQ-04: Read-only invocations, invocations in the primary checkout, and invocations outside version control succeed under either stance.
- [hard] REQ-05: Existing coverage that mutates from a linked checkout declares the stance it relies on rather than depending on an unstated default.

## Notes

The condition is evaluated at dispatch, before the repository mutation session is opened, so a
refused invocation is not a state change and appends nothing: the append-on-state-change
guarantee is preserved rather than excepted.

The session predicate is deliberately broader than the divergent-history hazard: an invocation
that writes only the shared control plane or machine-local runtime state still classifies as
mutating and refuses under the refusing stance. An over-refusal of that kind is the chosen
behaviour, not a defect.

planning.outcome: State-mutating dispatch refuses inside a linked checkout unless the stance or an explicit override permits it.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One dispatch-site condition consuming the already-produced detection, policy, and audit-record contracts, plus the focused new coverage and the stance declarations the refusing default forces onto existing linked-checkout tests.

title: Exact single-store read for cross-checkout comparison
description:
Storage owns a read that returns exactly the records one checkout's store holds — its issue
records and its event log — with no aggregation from version-control history or another
checkout.

## Background

The ordinary issue and index readers deliberately union the local store, versioned history,
and the primary checkout, which is the documented adopter-facing read model. A divergence
comparison needs the opposite: the records one store actually holds, because the union masks
exactly the one-sided records such a comparison exists to surface. Persistence access belongs
to the storage layer, so the exact read is a storage-owned operation that a command consumes.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A storage-owned read returns exactly the issue records and event records one checkout's store holds, with no fallback to versioned history or another checkout's store.
- [hard] REQ-02: A record held only by a different checkout's store does not appear in the read's result, proven by a test that would fail under the aggregating readers.
- [hard] REQ-03: The read is read-only, and it works against a checkout store other than the one the process runs in.
- [hard] REQ-04: The existing aggregated readers keep their documented behaviour unchanged.

## Notes

The exact read is a storage-owned operation addressed at an explicit store location, not a
method on the shared issue-store interface, so the in-memory implementation and its shared
behavioural contract are not engaged.

planning.outcome: Storage returns exactly what one checkout's store holds, unmasked by the aggregating read model.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One read-only storage operation beside readers whose aggregation it deliberately omits, with its non-masking property unit-proven.

title: Report divergent checkout stores
description:
A read-only check reports the issue records and event history one checkout's store holds and
the other does not, in both directions.

## Background

No command compares two checkouts' tracker stores today. The two existing names that sound
like they might belong to unrelated concepts: one reports membership labels disagreeing with
the dependency graph, the other checks branch ancestry against the upstream default. An
adopter recovering a divergent store therefore has no way to see what diverged. Issue records
do fall back across the local store, version-control history, and the primary checkout when
read, but the event log has no fallback at all, so a linked checkout's events are visible only
from inside it.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The check names issue records present in one checkout's store and absent from the other, in both directions, and writes to neither store.
- [hard] REQ-02: The check names event records held by one checkout's log and missing from the other, since event history has no cross-checkout read path.
- [hard] REQ-03: Records present in both stores but holding conflicting values are reported as conflicts, distinct from records present in only one place.
- [hard] REQ-04: The check reports no findings in the primary checkout, in a linked checkout whose store agrees with the primary, and outside version control.
- [hard] REQ-05: Machine-readable output carries the same findings as the rendered output, wrapped in the repository's list envelope.
- [hard] REQ-06: The worktree command reference states the check, its output shape, and what each finding class means.

## Notes

The comparison consumes the storage-owned exact single-store read; the command layer
performs no direct persistence access of its own. The check reads only. Recovering from a reported divergence is a separate concern, and this
surface deliberately offers no reconciliation.

planning.outcome: A read-only check reports the issue records and events one checkout holds without the other.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One read-only comparison over two store locations the detection primitive already resolves, with no mutation path to design.

footprint.uncertainty: whether the comparison lands inside the existing worktree command module or beside it is left to implementation

title: Converge the deletion refusal into the write policy
description:
The standalone secondary-checkout deletion refusal becomes a case of the general
linked-checkout write policy rather than a parallel variant.

## Background

Issue deletion carries its own unconditional secondary-checkout refusal, checked independently
of any policy and with its own detection mechanism. With a general write policy governing
state-mutating dispatch, a second, private refusal for one command is exactly the parallel
variant the repository's convention-convergence invariant names a defect.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Deletion inside a linked non-primary checkout is governed by the general write policy, and the independent unconditional check no longer exists as a separate mechanism.
- [hard] REQ-02: Under the refusing stance, deletion inside a linked checkout keeps its current outcome: it is refused with an explanation before any write.
- [hard] REQ-03: Under a permitting stance or an explicit override, deletion follows the general policy like every other state-mutating invocation.

planning.outcome: The standalone deletion refusal dissolves into the general linked-checkout write policy.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One special case removed in favour of a policy that already exists when this task starts, with the pinned deletion tests updated to declare their stance.

title: State the linked-checkout write stance in the worktree guides
description:
The adopter guides that teach the linked-checkout workflow state the write stance that
governs it and where a repository declares that stance.

## Background

The parallel-work tutorial and the multi-agent coordination guide teach mutation from a linked
checkout as the sanctioned workflow. With a refusing default governing that workflow, a reader
following either page in a repository that has declared nothing meets a refusal the pages
never mention, and the opt-in path the refusal names is undiscoverable from the only pages
that teach the workflow it governs.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The parallel-work tutorial states the stance that governs mutation inside a linked checkout and where a repository declares it, and every step it instructs succeeds under the stance it tells the reader to declare.
- [hard] REQ-02: The multi-agent coordination guide states the same stance where it presents linked-checkout writes as the sanctioned path.

planning.outcome: The worktree guides state the write stance and its declaration point, so their steps succeed as instructed.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One fact stated in the two pages that teach the governed workflow, against behaviour that already exists when this task starts.

title: Recovery guidance for divergent checkout stores
description:
Adopter guidance states a lossless recovery procedure for a divergent checkout store, and the
cleanup recipe for an abandoned checkout looks for unmerged tracker state before anything is
discarded.

## Background

The published cleanup recipe removes an abandoned checkout with a single version-control
command and then says only that leases expire. It says nothing about whether that checkout
holds tracker records committed nowhere else, which is the most plausible mechanical route to
permanently losing the only copy of issue and event history. Existing recovery material covers
merge conflicts inside one checkout, but nothing covers two checkouts whose stores diverged.
The event log already carries a union merge declaration, so disjoint event history survives a
merge; issue records do not, and need a stated decision point.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The procedure preserves both checkouts' issue records and both event logs before any reconciliation step, so no step can leave a record with a single copy.
- [hard] REQ-02: The procedure states how the event log's union merge behaviour keeps disjoint event history, and where issue records need a human decision instead.
- [hard] REQ-03: The procedure directs the reader to the read-only divergence check as its first step and states how to read each finding class.
- [hard] REQ-04: The cleanup recipe for an abandoned checkout checks for unmerged tracker state before removal and states what to do when that check reports findings.
- [hard] REQ-05: The parallel-work material links to the procedure from where it describes per-checkout tracker state, with each fact stated in one place rather than restated.

## Notes

The procedure composes version-control behaviour the repository already declares with the
read-only check; it introduces no reconciliation command of its own.

planning.outcome: Adopters recover a divergent checkout store losslessly and screen for unmerged state before discarding one.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: Two existing pages gain one procedure and one recipe safeguard over capabilities that already exist, with no code surface left open.

title: Regression coverage for gate evaluation durability
description:
An injected persistence failure during an automated gate evaluation proves that success is
reported only once the gate run, the issue gate status, and the event are durably recorded.

## Background

An adopter reported a gate evaluation printing success without a durable gate-run record. The
current automated path builds the issue update, the gate-run record, and the event into one
plan and applies them through the recovering two-phase-commit kernel before returning, so the
guarantee holds on that path; what is missing is coverage that would catch its regression.
Failure injection through the transaction kernel already exists and is used where gates are
defined, but never where a gate is run. The existing crashed-fixture helper is
initialization-specific and the command subprocess exposes no injector, so the coverage drives
the gate path in process with injected storage and then inspects the recovered repository from
a separate process.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A persistence failure injected during an automated gate evaluation returns failure rather than success.
- [hard] REQ-02: After that injected failure, a freshly opened repository reports the gate as not passed and holds no gate-run record for the failed attempt.
- [hard] REQ-03: A separate process reading the same repository after recovery reports the same gate status, proving the guarantee at the boundary an adopter uses rather than in process only.
- [hard] REQ-04: On the successful path, the gate run, the issue gate status, and the event are all readable once the evaluation returns.
- [hard] REQ-05: The manual attestation branch of gate evaluation is confirmed to propagate a persistence failure rather than reporting success, with coverage proving it.

## Notes

This adds no production code: the durability primitive already exists, and the value delivered
is the coverage that fails if it regresses.

planning.outcome: Injected persistence failure during a gate evaluation returns failure and leaves no passing gate record.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One failure-injection case follows an existing gate-definition pattern into the gate-run path, with no production change to design.

title: Surface swallowed postcheck failures
description:
An automated postcheck whose evaluation fails to persist surfaces that failure instead of
leaving the transition indistinguishable from a clean run.

## Background

The postcheck loop discards each checker result through an ignored return value, and the
comment above it claims failures are logged where the code at that site emits nothing. The
state machine stays correct — an unpassed gate keeps the issue out of the terminal state — but
the invocation returns ordinary success, so a persistence failure inside a postcheck leaves no
evidence anywhere. Which invocations reach this loop is not established: the primary
state-update path is a different function, and the one direct caller found transitions to a
rejected state.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The invocations that reach the postcheck loop are enumerated as part of this change, and the loop distinguishes a persistence failure from an ordinary checker failure.
- [hard] REQ-02: A persistence failure inside a postcheck reaches the caller rather than being discarded, and the invocation does not report unqualified success.
- [hard] REQ-03: An ordinary failing checker keeps its current outcome: the issue stays out of the terminal state and the invocation succeeds.
- [hard] REQ-04: The comment describing the loop's error handling matches what the code does.

## Notes

Whether the surfacing is a returned error or a reported warning depends on which invocations
reach the loop, so the enumeration settles that question before the surfacing is written.

planning.outcome: A postcheck persistence failure reaches the caller instead of being silently discarded.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One error path in one loop, with its caller set enumerated first so the surfacing shape is decided from evidence rather than guessed.

title: Typed remedy data on profile conflicts
description:
Each profile target conflict and each profile divergence carries a serializable remedy value
naming which resolutions apply, instead of encoding that knowledge only in the prose it
renders.

## Background

The conflict type already distinguishes its remedies exhaustively: it selects a different
prose constant per variant, and for at least one real adopter case one of the two candidate
remedies is invalid rather than merely less preferred. That knowledge exists as an exhaustive
match over typed values and is discarded the moment it becomes a sentence. The divergence type
is already serializable and schema-described; the conflict type is neither.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A typed remedy value names each resolution that applies to a conflict or a divergence, distinguishing restoring recorded content from capturing repository content, and marking capture as applicable only where capture is valid.
- [hard] REQ-02: The conflict type serializes, carrying its remedy beside the values that identify the conflict.
- [hard] REQ-03: The rendered prose derives from that same typed remedy, so a reader of the sentence and a reader of the data act on identical resolutions.
- [hard] REQ-04: Existing coverage asserting the rendered prose keeps passing, including the assertion that capture is named only where it applies.

## Notes

The remedy vocabulary is domain data on the conflict and divergence types. How it reaches a
command's output is a separate concern.

planning.outcome: Profile conflicts and divergences carry a serializable remedy naming which resolutions apply.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One exhaustive match already distinguishes the remedies, so the change turns existing branching into a typed value the prose then derives from.

title: Profile conflict output carries its remedy
description:
Profile refusals and divergences reach machine consumers as structured details and suggested
resolutions rather than as one flat sentence.

## Background

Two failure branches build their machine-readable output from the error's rendered text alone,
discarding the typed value behind it. The same output type already supports attached details
and suggestions, and two neighbouring profile subcommands already use it to carry structured
findings — so the pattern is proven on this exact surface and needs extending to the refusal
paths rather than inventing.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A refused profile publication emits its conflict code together with structured details naming each conflicting target, its conflict class, and its typed remedy.
- [hard] REQ-02: A reported divergence emits structured details naming each diverged target, its divergence class, and its typed remedy.
- [hard] REQ-03: Suggested resolutions accompany the details and name capture only where the remedy marks capture applicable.
- [hard] REQ-04: The failure code, the exit status, and the rendered human message of both paths keep their current content.
- [hard] REQ-05: Existing coverage reading these failures asserts the structured fields rather than the sentence alone.

## Notes

Coverage for this surface lives in the command-boundary suites, so the assertions run against
the process an adopter actually invokes.

planning.outcome: Profile refusals and divergences reach machine consumers with structured details plus suggested resolutions.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: Two failure branches gain the attachment pattern two neighbouring subcommands already use, with the pinned assertions extended alongside them.

title: Profile recovery guidance reference
description:
The canonical profile reference and the bridge's tool descriptions state the machine-readable
remedy contract, so an adopter reading prose and an agent reading data find the same
resolutions.

## Background

The profile reference already gives restore-versus-capture guidance in prose. Once that
distinction is available as data on refusals and divergences, the reference states the
contract rather than restating advice, and the error-code entry for a refused publication
points at it instead of carrying its own copy. The bridge's curated tool descriptions already
mention divergence and capture as a recovery choice, so they name where the structured remedy
appears.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The profile reference states the remedy vocabulary, which resolutions each conflict and divergence class carries, and where the structured form appears in machine-readable output.
- [hard] REQ-02: The error-code entry for a refused publication points at that guidance rather than repeating it.
- [hard] REQ-03: The bridge's tool descriptions name the structured remedy as the resolution source for a divergence and for a refusal.
- [hard] REQ-04: Each guidance fact has one home, with other pages citing it instead of restating it.

## Notes

The contract described here is already shipped by the time this lands, so no behaviour is
decided in prose.

planning.outcome: The profile reference and the bridge tool descriptions state the machine-readable remedy contract.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: Three prose surfaces state one contract that already ships, with no behaviour decided and no code path to design.

footprint.uncertainty: whether the bridge's pinned tool-inventory assertions cover the edited description strings is unconfirmed

title: Positional profile id for the show command
description:
The profile show command accepts an unambiguous positional profile id, translating it to an
identity selector inside its own dispatch.

## Background

Selecting a profile requires a tagged, repeatable selector naming either a recorded identity
or a package directory. A first invocation passing a bare profile id is rejected by the
argument parser's generic unexpected-argument message, which names the required flag but not
the tag syntax, so the correct form is not discoverable from the failure. The shared selector
parser serves the other lifecycle commands, whose contracts assert that they expose the
repeatable flag and nothing else, so the change stays inside this one command's arguments and
dispatch.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A single bare positional argument to the show command selects the recorded profile of that identity.
- [hard] REQ-02: A positional argument given together with the tagged selector flag is refused with a message naming both forms.
- [hard] REQ-03: An invalid positional value fails with a message naming the accepted selector forms rather than the parser's generic unexpected-argument text.
- [hard] REQ-04: The shared selector parser is unchanged, and the other lifecycle commands still expose the repeatable tagged selector alone.
- [hard] REQ-05: The command reference states the positional form beside the tagged form.

## Notes

The tagged form stays the general contract. The positional form is a first-invocation
convenience on the one read-only command where a bare identity is unambiguous.

planning.outcome: A bare positional id selects a recorded profile on the show command without touching the shared grammar.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One command's argument definition plus its own dispatch translation, with the schema assertion that pins its current shape updated in the same change.

title: Linked-checkout write-policy journey
description:
A linked checkout created by the test itself proves refusal, stance-based permission, and
the override audit record from the boundary an adopter invokes.

## Background

The reported field incident began in a linked worker checkout whose mutations silently built
a divergent store. An existing integration suite already creates real linked checkouts with
version-control commands, and it is the target with the most room for new modules under the
repository's test-target budget, so this coverage lands there rather than claiming a scarce
target slot.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Under the refusing stance, a state-mutating invocation inside a test-created linked checkout is rejected and leaves that checkout's store and event log unchanged.
- [hard] REQ-02: The same invocation succeeds under a permitting declared stance and emits no override record, and succeeds under an explicit per-invocation override leaving the durable override record behind.
- [hard] REQ-03: The refusal observed at this boundary carries the machine-readable facts the policy promises: the linked checkout, the refusing stance, and how to permit the operation.
- [hard] REQ-04: The coverage lands as modules of an existing test target and keeps the suite inside the repository's measured budgets.

planning.outcome: A live linked checkout proves refusal, permission, and the override audit record end to end.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One journey over the write-policy behaviours its prerequisite already ships, following an existing pattern for creating real linked checkouts inside tests.

title: Divergence and recovery journey
description:
A linked checkout with a deliberately diverged store proves the divergence report and the
lossless recovery procedure from the boundary an adopter invokes.

## Background

The reported field incident ended with issue and event history recoverable only from a
dangling commit. No artefact of that repository is preserved anywhere, so the reproduction is
built rather than restored: a test-created linked checkout diverges its store on purpose, and
the check and the documented procedure are then exercised exactly as an adopter would run
them.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: After a mutation inside the linked checkout, the divergence check run from the primary reports the diverged issue records and the disjoint events, and reports nothing once the two stores agree.
- [hard] REQ-02: The documented recovery procedure applied to that reproduction yields one store holding both checkouts' issue records and both event histories, with neither side overwritten.
- [hard] REQ-03: The coverage lands as modules of an existing test target and keeps the suite inside the repository's measured budgets.

planning.outcome: A deliberately diverged linked checkout proves the divergence report and lossless recovery end to end.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One journey over the divergence and recovery capabilities its prerequisite chain already ships, following the existing linked-checkout test pattern.
